title: The fourth and fifth ways
hook: degrees of goodness and order in nature; thinkers still argue about these

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second and third ways: a first cause, and something that exists of itself. Your line was why anything at all.

An arrow leaves the bow and crosses the whole field into the center of the target. The arrow knows nothing. It doesn't aim. It doesn't want the bullseye. And yet, from a good archer's hand, it gets there. That arrow is Thomas Aquinas's own picture, the last image in his five ways. Two are left. Today, walk them, then ask what an argument like this is for. Today's word: the fourth and fifth ways.
screen: `AN ARROW THAT DOESN'T AIM.` → `TWO WAYS LEFT.` → `WHAT IS AN ARGUMENT FOR?`

segments.voice: The fourth way starts from more and less. We call one act kinder than another, one answer truer, one life nobler. Thomas says more and less only make sense measured against a most. So there is something truest, best, noblest, and so most fully being, which causes the being and goodness in everything else. This, he says, we call God. His example shows his age: fire, the hottest thing, causing heat in all the rest. That's the science he learned. The point he's after is goodness, not fire. The fifth way is the arrow. Things without minds still act for an end. An acorn heads for oak. Rain falls, plants turn toward light, regularly, not by luck. But a thing with no mind can't head for a goal unless someone with a mind directs it, as the archer directs the arrow. So there is someone intelligent who directs natural things to their ends. This, he says, we call God. Notice what it's not: it isn't about how intricate a thing is, but how reliably mindless things lean toward a goal. The Psalm sings the same direction, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God." Now the arguing. Thomas meant these as real arguments, and readers, believing and not, still push on them: on the step from more to most, on whether nature's regularity needs a director. But Thomas called them ways. A way doesn't drag you. You walk it, weigh each step, and decide. He wrote them for beginners, in a book that states the other side first. An argument, for him, is an invitation to think, not a fist.
screen: `MORE AND LESS NEED A MOST.` · `MINDLESS THINGS ACT FOR AN END.` · `NOT INTRICACY, BUT DIRECTION.` · `A WAY HAS TO BE WALKED.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS SHEW FORTH THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Choose an argument you disagree with, about God or anything that matters, and walk it step by step, asking at each one whether it holds for you, until you find the exact step where you get off. Don't argue back; just notice that the argument can't make you do anything, only invite. If you pray, ask for an honest mind; if you don't, simply look at the spot where you stepped off.
The fourth and fifth ways. Thomas's arguments from degrees of goodness, which point to a most, and from order in nature, which points to a mind that directs.
screen: `THE FOURTH AND FIFTH WAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: arguments invite, not force. A way has to be walked. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Catholic classrooms the five ways are often taught as a set, with time given to the objections raised against them and to Thomas's own replies.

fork.setup: a friend tells you the fifth way doesn't convince them. what fits Thomas's own way of working?
options: tell them they just aren't thinking clearly.
state their objection fairly, then give your reply.

fork.reveal: the Summa puts the objections first and answers each one. even in the article on the five ways, Thomas states the case against God's existence before he replies.

chat.says: If Thomas's arguments for God are so good, why doesn't everyone who reads them believe?
options: He called them ways: an argument invites you to walk and weigh each step; it can't force anyone.
Thomas said anyone who rejects them is being dishonest, so the fault always lies with the reader.
Thomas never meant them as arguments; they were only poems to stir up feeling in believers.
chat.meaning: Thomas meant the five ways as real arguments, but called them ways: you walk each step and weigh it. An argument is an invitation, not a fist.

five ways.meaning: Thomas's five arguments that God exists

notes: ST I.2.3 fourth way paraphrased: more and less said by resemblance to a maximum; something truest, best, noblest, and so uttermost being; the maximum in a genus causes all in that genus (fire and heat, which Thomas takes from Aristotle); 'this we call God'. Fifth way: things lacking intelligence act for an end, always or nearly always the same way; directed by one with knowledge, as the arrow by the archer; 'this being we call God'. Confirm.
The acorn, rain and plants are the script's examples; Thomas speaks of natural bodies generally.
'Not intricacy, but direction' distinguishes the fifth way from later design arguments without naming them; confirm the framing.

'Readers, believing and not, still push on them' and 'thinkers, believers and not, still argue about them' are general statements from the outline hook ('thinkers still argue about these'); no counts given.
Douay-Rheims Psalm 18:2: confirm exact wording and verse numbering.
Original: ST I.2.3 reads 'Deum esse quinque viis probari potest'. Confirm.
